title: I am the worst of all
hook: Kabir says he is the worst, and everyone else is good (Kabir salok, ang 1364)

segments.voice: Yesterday, bichar, and your line, reflect, don't dismiss. Which idea did you give one honest minute? Today Kabir turns that same reflection on himself. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

A group chat goes sour. Someone said something careless, someone else snapped, and now everyone is typing out exactly who did what wrong. Screenshots. Receipts. Every message pointing outward. Now set beside that scene a couplet, two short lines, from the back of the Guru Granth Sahib, where Kabir's saloks are gathered. It points the other way entirely. It's so blunt it can sound almost wrong on first hearing. Today: I am the worst of all.
screen: `A GROUP CHAT GOES SOUR.` → `EVERY FINGER POINTS OUT.` → `A COUPLET POINTS IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the salok. Kabir, it begins, I am the worst of all; apart from me, everyone is good. And the second line: whoever comes to see it this way is my friend. That's the whole of it. Two lines. Now, it would be easy to hear this as someone who hates himself. Sikh teachers read it differently. They hear humility, the low, open place where water gathers. Kabir isn't keeping a score where he loses. He's refusing to keep the score at all. Think about where the eye goes in that group chat. Outward, to everyone else's faults, because that's where the eye naturally points. Farid's couplet, a little over two weeks back on this path, said look inside your own collar. Kabir's salok turns the same way and follows it all the way down. Look at your own part first, so carefully that by the time you're done, you've run out of energy for judging anyone else. And the second line matters as much as the first. Whoever sees it this way is my friend. So it's not a lonely practice. It's the ground of a friendship: two people who've both stopped pointing. Guru Nanak, in Raag Suhi, says we are not good, and no one is bad. That's the shape of it. Not crushing yourself. Just taking yourself off the judge's bench. Here's the surprise in it. The salok says I am the worst, but the line it hands us to carry is the other half: everyone else is good. The point isn't the low opinion of yourself. It's the generous eye it frees up for everyone else.
screen: `I AM THE WORST OF ALL.` · `HUMILITY, NOT SELF-HATRED.` · `WHOEVER SEES IT SO IS MY FRIEND.` · `WE ARE NOT GOOD, NO ONE IS BAD.` · then, large: `EVERYONE ELSE IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your own fault first. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one recent friction: an argument, a cold silence, a sharp text. Before you think about what they did, find your part. Even a small one. A tone, a delay, an assumption. Name it to yourself, plainly, without punishing yourself for it. Then notice how the other person looks once your part is on the table. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and let it be gentle. The bell holds the time.
Salok. Kabir's short couplet in the Guru Granth Sahib: apart from me everyone is good, and whoever sees it this way is my friend.
Your line: everyone else is good. Today, the next time someone gets on your nerves, look for your own part before you name theirs. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Sikhs read and sing Kabir's saloks, gathered near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and teachers use this one to teach nimrata, humility, alongside the Gurus' own hymns.

fork.setup: you're Kabir, writing two short lines about faults. where do you point?
options: at the others, so they can improve.
at yourself: I am the worst, everyone else is good.
fork.reveal: Kabir points in, and then adds: whoever sees it this way is my friend.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint with very low self-esteem.
what it means: humility. look at your own part first, and the eye you free up sees others as good.
what a scholar hears: the salok's second line makes it a friendship, and it sits beside Guru Nanak's we are not good, and no one is bad.
recall: the Sufi sitting in Farid's seat

notes: Salok paraphrased; confirm Ang 1364 and the rendering.
Echo from Guru Nanak, Raag Suhi, Ang 728 ('ham nahi change bura nahi koe'): confirm Ang and attribution.
'Sikh readers don't take it that way. They hear humility' is a general reading claim; confirm.
'The low, open place where water gathers' is a writer's image for humility, not attributed to the text; confirm acceptable.
